articles.title: States leading nation on the biggest education battles gripping classrooms revealed in first-ever report
articles.summary: The Defending Education report ranks Tennessee first among all 50 states on parental rights, DEI, gender identity and public school policies.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The escalating battle over what children should be taught in public schools continues to drive America's culture wars, and a new report ranks every state on some of the most contentious issues affecting today's classrooms. Red states dominated the ranking, which measures all 50 states and Washington, D.C., on issues spanning parental rights, diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), gender and sexuality, teacher and union policies, and foreign influence, according to Defending Education's first-ever Rankings on Integrity in State Education, released Thursday. Tennessee claimed the top spot, followed by Alabama, Florida, North Carolina and Iowa, while Washington, D.C., ranked last, followed by Rhode Island, California, Oregon and Illinois. The rankings do not account for test scores or graduation rates. Instead, the report said it is designed to show how states are approaching hot-button issues as parents demand greater transparency in their children's education. DOJ LAWSUIT TARGETS ALLEGED SCHOOL ‘SECRET GENDER TRANSITIONS’ POLICIES THAT KEEP PARENTS IN THE DARK "For the first time, parents have a single resource to see how their state handles the issues they've voiced concerns about over the last five years, empowering them to evaluate local schools and hold leaders accountable at the ballot box," Paul Runko, senior director of strategic initiatives at Defending Education, said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Of the report's five categories, the parental rights category ended in a four-way tie, with North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and West Virginia earning the top spot. Each was awarded points for policies that give parents more say over student gender transitions, sex education instruction and whether their children participate in those lessons. Georgia, Mississippi, North Carolina and South Carolina, all red states, received perfect scores on teacher policies. According to the report, laws governing teacher unions, strikes and collective bargaining, along with work authorization requirements, were key factors in the scoring. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS Iowa, Missouri and West Virginia topped the report's DEI category after receiving high marks for laws restricting DEI initiatives and other policies related to restorative justice, teacher diversity and antisemitism. Another major flashpoint in education has been a growing conversation on gender identity and transgender athletes competing in women's sports. The report examined state policies blocking LGBTQ-specific curriculum, restricting transgender athlete participation, and state nondiscrimination and anti-bullying laws related to gender identity, finding Alabama, Florida and Indiana tied for the highest scores. But the report went further than policies shaping the classroom. Seven red states received perfect scores for laws limiting Chinese government influence in education, including Confucius Institutes, China-backed language and cultural education centers. Alabama, Florida, Indiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas aced the category. In another statement to Fox News Digital, Dr. Terry Stoops, director of government affairs at Defending Education, congratulated the frontrunners. EXCLUSIVE: HOUSE COMMITTEE PROBES CHICAGO PUBLIC SCHOOLS OVER HIDING 'GENDER AFFIRMATION' FROM PARENTS "If your state is at the top of Defending Education's rankings, congratulations!" he said. "You live in a state with public school policies that prioritize sound academics over shameless antics." Stoops also blamed elected leaders for the lowest-scoring states, accusing them of having "sacrificed educational excellence at the altar of social justice." "For parents in bottom-feeder states who value rigor over ridiculousness, the choice is either fight or flight," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Despite more blue states embracing DEI and social justice policies, the report said it wants parents to have a clearer picture of where their state stands on education and how those policies could impact their children and future generations.

articles.title: 10 Democrat-held House seats most likely to flip
articles.summary: As the midterm landscape grows more favorable for Democrats, Republicans are still poised for key pickups in the fight for House control. Forecasters have shifted a slate of House races away from Republicans in recent weeks amid voter frustration with President Trump and the GOP’s handling of the economy, immigration and the war in Iran, fueling…
articles.body:
As the midterm landscape grows more favorable for Democrats, Republicans are still poised for key pickups in the fight for House control.

Forecasters have shifted a slate of House races away from Republicans in recent weeks amid voter frustration with President Trump and the GOP’s handling of the economy, immigration and the war in Iran, fueling Democrats’ hopes of clawing back power on Capitol Hill.

But there are still several blue House seats that could flip this fall, particularly in states where Republican-friendly redistricting made key districts tougher for Democrats — and every race counts as Republicans expand their 218-seat majority and buck current forecasts that they could ultimately gain nothing from this cycle’s redrawn maps.

Ratings are changing quickly, and forecasters differ in just how competitive they consider the country’s top races. Here are 10 of the Democrat-held House seats that are most likely to flip in November.

Republicans are very likely to pick up the newly drawn 2nd District in Alabama after the Supreme Court’s spring ruling weakened the Voting Rights Act , ultimately allowing Southern states to pass new House maps favorable to the GOP.

The high court’s initial decision in 2023 to strike down a GOP-approved House map paved the way for Alabama to create a new congressional map with a second Black-majority House district for the 2024 election. Proponents argued that the state’s Black population made up close to a third of the state, but the lines essentially packed Black voters into one district.

Litigation, however, wound all the way up to the high court again — and ultimately reversed the new changes, allowing a more GOP-favorable House map to be used in the 2026 cycle.

The decision directly impacts Rep. Shomari Figures (D-Ala.), who was elected under the 2024 maps in a House district that stretched east to west in southern Alabama and included Montgomery. He’s facing Republican Rhett Marques.

The district now hugs the southeastern corner of the state. The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report’s partisan voting index puts the seat at a plus-seven Republican advantage.

Florida jumped into the redistricting war earlier this year at Trump’s urging, with aims of expanding Republicans’ 20-8 majority to a 24-4 advantage in the congressional delegation.

Democratic Rep. Darren Soto has held the central Florida 9th District for roughly a decade but now faces a tough fight against Republican Dan Green after gerrymandering gave the GOP a leg up.

Cook Political Report says Democrats still “have an outside shot” of holding the seat, but redistricting gave the GOP a major edge. It’s rated likely Republican, a step short of being solidly red — while Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) rates it even closer to Democrats as “lean” Republican.

Moderate Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz is also running for reelection in a Sunshine State district made tougher by redistricting.

The new 25th Congressional District, which stretches from South Beach to Delray Beach, took in portions of the old 23rd and 24th districts, shifting it from a seat that former Vice President Kamala Harris won by 5 points to one that would have favored Trump by 9 points in 2024.

The two-term lawmaker easily beat a progressive challenger in South Florida’s summer primaries but now faces Trump-backed Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer (R) in the general election.

Cook Political Report considers the race a toss-up, but DDHQ now considers it to lean Democratic — a potential bright spot for Democrats seeking to stem GOP redistricting gains.

The Supreme Court’s decision to weaken the Voting Rights Act has also created a new opportunity in the Pelican State, where Republicans passed a new map.

The same Supreme Court ruling in 2023 that allowed Alabama to create a new Black-majority House district also paved the way for Louisiana to create a new congressional map with a second Black-majority district.

Rep. Cleo Fields (D-La.) was the beneficiary of that decision, representing the newer 6th District — a sprawling area that crisscrosses from the Shreveport area to Baton Rouge.

But with the high court’s more recent ruling dismantling the Voting Rights Act, Republicans look poised to pick that seat back up.

The 6th District drawn for this year’s midterms is more compact in southeastern Louisiana and Cook Political Report’s partisan voting index gives Republicans a 16-point edge there. Notably, the election for Louisiana’s 6th District is on Dec. 12, with the primary slated for Nov. 3.

Rep. Jared Golden’s (D-Maine) decision to opt against another run in the House has offered Republicans a rare opportunity to take back the GOP-friendly 2nd District in the Pine Tree State.

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage (R), a longtime supporter of the president, is running against progressive state auditor Matt Dunlap for the open seat.

The seat last elected a Republican in 2016, and the district went for Trump by 9 points in 2024, according to The Downballot . Cook Political Report rates the seat as “likely Republican.”

Tennessee Republicans made a last-minute redraw of their House map after the Supreme Court’s blockbuster spring ruling, targeting Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen’s (Tenn.) Memphis-area seat. He opted to retire after the GOP’s redistricting push.

A district that previously went for Harris by 21 points now has a Cook Political Report partisan voting index of a 9-point advantage for the GOP. Cohen was already contending with a serious primary challenge from state Rep. Justin Pearson (D).

Now, the district — drawn as an “L” that runs through more than half of the state’s southern border before curving upward into Middle Tennessee — is poised to be represented by Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor.

Democratic Rep. Don Davis’s district was redrawn last year to favor Republicans as North Carolina joined the nationwide redistricting fight.

Davis now faces a 2024 rematch against Republican Laurie Buckhout two years after he defeated her by less than 2 points.

As Davis won a second term, the northeastern seat sided with Trump by 3 points. Under the new lines, the district favors Trump, who’s backing Buckhout, by 11 points.

Cook Political Report rates the race as more favorable for Republicans, calling Davis “without a doubt, the most vulnerable House Democrat in the country.” DDHQ has labeled it a toss-up.

Rep. Al Green’s (D) seat in Texas’s 9th Congressional District has merged with the empty blue seat vacated by the late Rep. Sylvester Turner (D), yielding a more conservative 9th District in the suburbs of east Houston for the next Congress.

The old 9th District went to Harris by a whopping 44 points, according to The Downballot, while the redrawn district would have backed Trump by 20 points.

But there’s a bright spot for Democrats: Hispanic voters, who make up roughly 6 in 10 Texans in the new Houston exurbs district, are turning away from Trump amid economic frustrations, and could drive up Democrats’ numbers in the red stronghold.

Cook Political Report and DDHQ both rate the race as likely Republican, after moving the race toward Democrats last week. Democrat Leticia Gutierrez is facing the GOP’s Alex Mealer for the seat, after Green unsuccessfully ran in the Democratic primary for the 18th District.

One of Republicans’ best Texas pickup opportunities is in the 32nd District, where Republican attorney Jace Yarbrough faces Democrat Dan Barrios.

The current seat, which stretches from the Dallas suburbs into east Texas, favored Harris by more than 20 points in 2024, but the redrawn district would have gone to Trump by roughly 18 points.

The current district, based in Dallas, is held by Democratic Rep. Julie Johnson, who will be out of the House next year after an unsuccessful bid for reelection in the new, safely blue 33rd District, where former Rep. Colin Allred (D-Texas) is all but assured a comeback.

Cook Political Report rates the race as solidly Republican, while DDHQ considers it likely Republican.

Carlos De La Cruz (R), the brother of GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz (Texas), faces Democrat Johnny Garcia for yet another Lone Star State seat reshaped by GOP-friendly redistricting.

Rep. Greg Casar (D) has called the dismantling of his 35th District through redistricting the “illegal voter suppression of Black and Latino Central Texans.” He’s now running in the new 37th District, teeing up a wide-open race for his redrawn seat.

Now a Trump plus-10 seat, the 35th District is within Republicans’ reach. But, as with the 9th Congressional District, Hispanic voters make up more than half of the new, suburban San Antonio district, and the bloc’s upset with Trump could make the seat more of a lift for the GOP.

Cook Political Report rates the race as lean Republican, after shifting the race toward Democrats last week, while DDHQ rates it a toss-up.

articles.title: GOP wrestles with rising data center backlash weeks before midterms
articles.summary: Republicans are growing increasingly worried that data centers are a liability in the midterms, as concerns over higher power bills tied to the facilities turn into a pocketbook issue for voters. The debate over the issue was on full display Wednesday, after Senate Democrats blocked legislation championed by Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) — who is…
articles.body:
Republicans are growing increasingly worried that data centers are a liability in the midterms, as concerns over higher power bills tied to the facilities turn into a pocketbook issue for voters.

The debate over the issue was on full display Wednesday, after Senate Democrats blocked legislation championed by Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) — who is in a competitive reelection bid against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) — that would require states and some electric utilities to consider a standard under which data centers would have to pay for additional costs caused by their large power demand.

The stalled legislation puts Republicans in a political bind as they seek to address voter concerns over data centers while navigating the White House’s embrace of the facilities. President Trump touted data centers during a meeting with tech CEOs on Tuesday, saying they “are going to be very popular.”

Lawmakers are poised to take a second crack at seeking to ensure data center energy costs aren’t passed down to consumers, but it likely won’t be taken up until after the November elections.

“Politicians in both parties are now figuring out that the voters expect them to either oppose data center expansion or to have … some very, very serious checks on how they’re going to be built out, and it is a box that has to be checked correctly, or it can be disqualifying to voters,” GOP analyst Rob Stutzman said.

And for Republicans in particular, the White House’s stance only compounds that political challenge as the GOP seeks to retain its majority in November. Democrats are forecasted to flip the House and potentially the Senate amid voter anger over cost of living and the Trump administration’s record.

“I just think that when the president weighs in on something and says something … has to be good, or ‘We all are going to like them’ — that muddles things a little bit, right?” GOP strategist Amy Koch said. “It’s hard to be nuanced with a president who has no nuance.”

Democrats have also seized on data centers’ rising unpopularity among Americans to attack Republicans on the issue.

In the Ohio Senate race, Brown has highlighted Husted’s support for data center tax breaks during the Republican’s tenure as lieutenant governor, suggesting he was “the point man to bring these data centers to Ohio.”

The National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), in an August memo obtained by NewsNation, wrote that, “More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck. If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one.”

The NRSC warned that Brown’s approach was working, saying his messaging “is significantly more effective than traditional messaging tracts, as it introduces new information on a highly relevant, emerging topic. This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.”

Earlier this week in New York, Democrat Cait Conley accused incumbent Rep. Mike Lawler (R) of not supporting a moratorium on data centers during a News12 debate. Lawler’s campaign manager Ciro Riccardi previously told New York Focus that the congressman “believes local residents should decide what gets built in their community.”

“Municipalities should use every tool available to protect residents’ quality of life and keep the cost off ratepayers, who already pay a third more for electricity than New Jersey and Pennsylvania because of Albany’s energy policies,” Riccardi added.

Lawler is running in a battleground district that is rated as a toss-up by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report.

Koch said that GOP candidates are trying to strike a nuanced tone with data centers, much as they have with artificial intelligence — avoiding a rush to regulate an emerging industry while acknowledging the potential costs to communities.

“I think the Republican approach to it — setting aside Trump saying everyone’s going to like data centers — no one’s going to like data centers. That’s silly,” Koch said. “But understanding that there … is a need for data centers, and let’s do it in a way that’s smart.”

“Let’s do it in a way that’s innovative. Let’s … push the companies to make sure that … when they’re putting them up, they’re well needed, that they’re actually needed, that they’re doing them in a way that is responsible,” Koch continued.

Some Republicans, however, have sought to highlight the economic benefits of hosting such facilities.

Rep. Rich McCormick (R-Ga.), who is expected to cruise to victory in the race for his ruby red seat, told Newsmax’s “Wake Up America” on Wednesday that “if you don’t want a data center, that’s fine, don’t have one.”

“But just realize they’re not going to use your water, they’re going to keep your electricity rate low, they’re going to pay for your teachers your schools your roads, most likely your property taxes, you’re gonna have more jobs,” McCormick said. “It’s going to be an amazing thing to have in your neighborhood.”

Rachel Frazin and Julia Shapero contributed to this repor t.

articles.title: Senate adjourns until November with Republicans fearful of losing majority
articles.summary: The Senate adjourned for the midterm election on Wednesday night despite having a big pile of unfinished business on its plate, as vulnerable Republicans were ready to get back to their home states to campaign amid growing fears that they may lose their majority in the upper chamber. Senators adjourned after voting to confirm Keith…
articles.body:
The Senate adjourned for the midterm election on Wednesday night despite having a big pile of unfinished business on its plate, as vulnerable Republicans were ready to get back to their home states to campaign amid growing fears that they may lose their majority in the upper chamber.

Senators adjourned after voting to confirm Keith Sonderling, President Trump’s nominee to serve as secretary of the Labor Department.

They left Washington without acting on three Congressional Review Act resolutions to waive California regulations that some Republicans wanted to pass before the extended recess.

Senators aren’t scheduled to return to the Capitol until the week of Nov. 9, leaving many top priorities in limbo until after the Nov. 3 election.

Those priorities include permitting reform, the annual defense authorization bill, the extension of expired surveillance authorities under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) and other high-profile items.

“It breaks my heart. It’s bad planning. We should have started after we passed One Big Beautiful Bill [in July of last year], planning what we wanted to do and how we were going to get it done,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said of the Senate adjourning.

Kennedy also warned the failure to finish up the Congressional Review Act resolutions on California-related regulatory waivers would add to the logjam in November and December.

But vulnerable Republican senators, such as Sens. Dan Sullivan (Alaska), Roger Marshall (Kan.) and Pete Ricketts (Neb.), are eager to get back on the campaign trail.

So is Republican Sen. Susan Collins (Maine), another top Democratic target, who was hoping to get a vote on her bipartisan bill to cap the monthly out-of-pocket cost of insulin at $35 before the election.

Collins acknowledged she had a busy month of campaigning in Maine ahead of her as she left the Capitol late Wednesday.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has made it clear that he thinks his GOP colleagues can help themselves by getting back to their home states as soon as possible to make the argument to voters that they deserve six more years in Washington.

On the Democratic side, Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) has a competitive race in Georgia, though strategists in both parties think he’s pulling away from the Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins.

“I think everybody’s nervous about their races,” Kennedy said. “It’s a weird year. I don’t know how these things are going to turn out.”

“I’ve done polling in my own state, and it’s a pretty red state, but people all across the political spectrum are very unsettled,” he added.

An Emerson College Polling survey released last week showed Democrats with an 11-point lead on the generic congressional ballot. The survey of 1,000 likely voters conducted from Sept. 21-22 showed Democrats with 53 percent support and Republicans with 42 percent support.

Kennedy noted it was a struggle to convince GOP leaders just to bring senators back to Washington this week to vote on two bills sponsored by Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Ricketts — the Ratepayer Protection Act and the Stop Insider Trading Act, respectively.

“We had to raise fresh hell just to get a vote on Sen. Husted’s bill,” Kennedy said.

Husted’s bill would ask states to consider new standards to shield taxpayers from paying the costs of upgrading energy and water infrastructure to accommodate data centers while Ricketts’s bill would have banned members of Congress from buying new publicly traded stocks.

Democrats blocked both measures by party-line votes on Wednesday.

When the Senate reconvenes in November, Republicans plan to tee up a vote on a permitting reform deal announced by Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Chair Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.).

Senators could have stayed in town to finish drafting the deal and possibly voted on it in October.

That may have allowed them to tout a major accomplishment to constituents, but they decided the next few weeks would be better spent talking to voters at home.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said senators in tough races wanted to get out of town as soon as possible with Election Day fast approaching.

“I think we’ll have a net loss. I think it’s unlikely we’d have the same numbers. The margins will be thinner,” he said.

He predicted that Senate Republican losses will be “manageable” if “we let candidates execute down the stretch.”

Tillis warned that keeping vulnerable incumbent senators in Washington comes at a high political cost.

“Every time you’re here, it’s a fundraiser you can’t host or it’s a town hall you can’t speak at. We need to get them back in the state. Invariably, the people who want to stick here, they all have one thing in common: They’re not up [for reelection] this cycle,” he said.

Republicans say that getting through the pile of unfinished work awaiting them in November and December will be a daunting task. After planned votes on the permitting reform bill, there’s little consensus on what comes next.

Senate Agriculture Committee Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) is pushing for the Senate to finish the long-stalled farm bill before Christmas.

“The majority leader is one of our most active members on the committee, and he’s committed to getting it done,” Boozman said of the farm bill. “The farm bill’s a priority.”

Meanwhile, Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) wants to make both the annual National Defense Authorization Act and an emergency supplemental defense spending package top priorities.

The leaders of the Senate Intelligence Committee want to take up legislation extending the expanded surveillance authorities under Section 702 of FISA that lapsed in June.

Also in the mix are the 12 annual appropriations bills.

Government funding is due to expire on Dec. 11. That sets up a high-stakes negotiation to avoid another government shutdown after Thanksgiving.

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) is pushing for a marathon series of votes on a budget resolution in the lame-duck to unlock the process for moving a third budget reconciliation package.

“That’s where I’ll be working at,” he said.

Johnson said he’s worked closely with House Budget Committee Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas) to lay the groundwork for moving a budget reconciliation package after the election.

Debating and voting on the preliminary budget resolution and then tackling a follow-up reconciliation package could easily consume a couple weeks of the Senate’s schedule.

Some Republicans may also insist on voting on the three Congressional Review Act resolutions — which were tentatively on the agenda for this week — in November or December.

The impending traffic jam of priorities has Republicans skeptical about getting much done at all in the lame-duck session.

“It’s going to be our golden era,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) quipped when asked if Republicans were punting too many items into November and December.

The Senate is scheduled to be in regular session only eight days in November and 14 days in December — counting Fridays, which aren’t typically workdays in the upper chamber.

The Senate voted 53-47 along party lines Wednesday afternoon to advance Sonderling’s nomination to head the Labor Department. About 10 hours later, weary senators returned to the Capitol for a final confirmation vote on the nominee after Democrats agreed to shorten the debate time on the floor.

Sonderling was confirmed shortly before midnight by a vote of 47 to 41.

Republican and Democratic senators spent part of Wednesday evening battling over requests for unanimous consent to advance bipartisan bills.

Johnson objected to a request by Sens. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) to pass a bill to eliminate pocket rescissions after the Trump administration advanced a request last week to cancel nearly $1 billion in funding already appropriated by Congress.

Sen. Rand Paul (R-Utah) objected to a request by Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) to pass by unanimous consent the Kids Online Safety Act, which is designed to protect minors who use social media platforms.

articles.title: Lawler trails Conley in battleground New York House contest: Poll
articles.summary: Democratic candidate Cait Conley inched ahead of incumbent Rep. Mike Lawler (R) in New York’s 17th Congressional District House race, up two percentage points in polling results released Thursday. articles.body:
Democratic candidate Cait Conley inched ahead of incumbent Rep. Mike Lawler (R) in New York’s 17th Congressional District House race, up two percentage points in polling results released Thursday.

The Emerson College and PIX11 survey found around 48 percent of likely voters in the district supported Conley, while 46 percent backed the Republican lawmaker. The remaining respondents were still undecided less than five weeks out from the November election.

The Democrat’s lead notably fell within the poll’s almost 5 percent margin of error.

The survey found a slight decrease in Lawler’s favorability among voters in his district since October 2024. Ten percent of respondents in the September survey said they had “never heard of” their congressman.

Lawler was first elected to represent New York’s 17th District in 2022, which includes the lower Hudson Valley in the southern part of the state. The Republican has touted his legislative record on the campaign trail, including his support for President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Conley, a retired Army combat veteran, has campaigned on lowering healthcare costs, banning stock trading for members of Congress and placing restrictions on energy rate increases.

In a debate earlier this week hosted by News12 in Long Island, the two candidates sparred over federal immigration enforcement operations, data centers and the Trump administration’s tariff fights with trading partners like Canada.

In one heated exchange between the candidates over a question on American aid to Israel, Lawler argued that this financial support is in the interest of the U.S. and its troops in the region.

He also pushed back against criticism of Israel’s actions in Gaza during the debate, saying, “They have not committed a genocide.”

A majority of respondents in the Emerson poll, 52 percent, said they opposed the U.S. military operations against Iran — including 83 percent of Democrats, 15 percent of Republicans and 44 percent of independent voters.

The poll also asked voters in the district about the top issue facing New York. Thirty-one percent named economic conditions, while 23 percent answered with “threats to democracy,” 13 percent indicated immigration issues and 12 percent selected housing affordability concerns.

The survey was conducted from Sept. 27 to 29 among 400 likely voters with a margin of error of approximately 4.9 percentage points. PIX11 is owned by Nexstar, which also owns The Hill.

articles.title: Biden-era federal prosecutor hit with criminal investigation referral over alleged false statements to FBI
articles.summary: A criminal referral sent to the Justice Department alleges ex-prosecutor Jina Choi misled FBI agents about her role in the IRL startup probe.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — A former senior federal prosecutor who served in the Biden administration has been hit with a criminal investigation referral asking the Justice Department to look into whether she misled federal agents about her role in an investigation, Fox News Digital has learned. Jina Choi joined the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California in late 2023, shortly after which Biden-appointed U.S. Attorney Ismail Ramsey tapped her to lead its Corporate and Securities Fraud Section, which handles major corporate and securities cases across the Bay Area, including Silicon Valley. Before joining the office, however, Choi had represented IRL, a social-media startup co-founded by Abraham Shafi. The company was built around organizing and connecting people through events. IRL shut down in 2023 after a board-directed investigation concluded that 95% of its users were likely bots, a finding Shafi disputed. Shafi was later indicted in 2025 on federal fraud and obstruction charges. The referral represents an unusually aggressive challenge to the conduct of a former prosecutor involved in the broader matter. FEDERAL JUDGE REFERS PHILADELPHIA DA LARRY KRASNER TO DOJ FOR POSSIBLE CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION Cully Stimson, acting director of the Heritage Foundation’s Legal Policy Center and himself a former federal prosecutor, told Fox News Digital that, while it is common for defense teams to attack prosecutors, resorting to a criminal investigation referral is rare. The referral, sent on Tuesday by a lawyer Shafi retained separately from his defense, turns on whether Choi remained involved in the IRL investigation after joining the U.S. Attorney’s Office despite being screened from the matter because of her prior representation of the company. The Justice Department generally has no obligation to respond to referrals like this. Prosecutors said Choi was walled off from the federal investigation involving IRL and Shafi. But Shafi’s lawyer now alleges that internal communications and an FBI interview report show she remained involved in the matter and later understated that involvement to federal agents. JIM JORDAN SAYS HOUSE WEIGHING CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF JACK SMITH FOR ALLEGEDLY LYING TO CONGRESS The FBI declined to comment when reached by Fox News Digital. In the criminal referral sent to the Justice Department on Tuesday, Shafi’s lawyer asked federal authorities to investigate whether Choi made false statements about her role in the investigation into IRL. The federal investigation into IRL predated Choi’s arrival at the U.S. Attorney’s Office. Prosecutors have said she was screened from the matter because of her prior representation of the company. Shafi’s defense claims to have obtained internal emails sent by Choi as well as FBI interview memoranda recounting a conversation she had with federal agents from the prosecution. Shafi’s lawyer argues the documents contradict Choi’s account to agents. NEW FEDERAL GRAND JURY SUBPOENA ISSUED TO FORMER JAMES COMEY ADVISOR IN LEAK INVESTIGATION: SOURCES While Choi’s communications are quoted or described in public court filings, the government filed the underlying email exhibits under seal or as sealed exhibit slip sheets. As a result, the public cannot independently inspect the original documents or assess their full context. Choi worked for IRL as outside counsel before joining the U.S. Attorney’s Office, according to court filings. During this time, Shafi’s defense alleged in its motion to dismiss the case against him that Choi attempted to get federal authorities to target Shafi to shield other stakeholders at the firm. The government denied this characterization, acknowledging that she advocated that the firm itself not be targeted, but disputing that she wanted the government to go after Shafi. The tech founder’s defense argues that Choi’s prior representation of IRL created a conflict of interest. Prosecutors have said she was walled off from the investigation because of that prior relationship. As of publishing, no ruling has been made finding that Choi operated under a conflict of interest that warrants dismissal. Shafi’s lawyer argues that documents they obtained tell a different story. ODNI SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRALS TO DOJ FOR EX-IG, WHISTLEBLOWER TIED TO TRUMP IMPEACHMENT The FBI, which was investigating the Shafi case, interviewed Choi in July and questioned her about her role in the IRL investigation, according to the referral. Choi allegedly told agents that she did "not have any kind of role in the investigation." An internal message purportedly obtained by the defense, however, quotes her as saying, "I talked to [her predecessor]] and I wanted to see if it would be ok to add [him] to the IRL team to help move it along." In other instances, documents obtained by the defense allegedly show that she inquired about the name of the FBI agent working on the IRL case and that she sent press coverage of the case against Shafi to other prosecutors. At one point during her FBI interview, Shafi's lawyer claims Choi said that she was not aware "who was assigned to the case team." PROSECUTOR OUSTED AFTER ALLEGED ROMANCE WITH ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SEX-CRIME SUSPECT: 'PATTERN OF MISCONDUCT' According to the criminal investigation referral, Choi "admitted keeping a written case tracker on which ‘the SHAFI investigation was listed.’" The defense claims that the U.S. Attorney’s Office refused to turn over the case tracker by describing it as a "privileged and internal work product." Shafi was charged with wire fraud, securities fraud and obstruction a few months after Choi left the U.S. Attorney’s Office. The charges stem from allegations that he misled investors by misrepresenting user growth on his platform. Prosecutors allege that he used paid advertising to attract people to IRL, then passed off the resulting growth as organic while raising about $170 million from investors. He also stands accused of misusing investors’ funds for clothing, home furnishings, travel, hotels and wedding-related costs. The founder’s lawyer argues that Choi’s alleged false statements to federal agents, coupled with her prior representation of IRL, taint the charges against Shafi. JACK SMITH DOUBLES DOWN AGAINST GOP ACCUSATIONS HE LIED UNDER OATH Shafi’s defense has a strong incentive to prove that Choi acted improperly, as doing so could seriously derail the prosecution of their client. "Here, the defense's allegations are troubling if true, because if their allegations end up being true, there was spillage," Stimson told Fox News Digital. "And that would mean some other members of that office are therefore conflicted, and it could result in the entire office being conflicted if a judge found that the taint was so bad that it permeated the whole office." Stimson also said that, in his experience, individual U.S. Attorneys’ Offices generally operate with significant independence on casework, cautioning against attributing Choi’s alleged conduct to the Biden administration more broadly. As of publishing, Choi has not been charged with any crime or disciplined for any professional misconduct in connection with the Shafi prosecution. articles.title: Pro-life group says mail-order abortion pills violate federal law, urges Trump admin to take action
articles.summary: The Restoration of America Foundation urges Attorney General Todd Blanche to enforce the Comstock Act against mail-order abortion pill shipments.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: A pro-life group has released a new report calling on the Trump administration to take action against mail-order abortion drugs, arguing that it can enforce a 19th-century federal law to crack down on abortion pill shipments. In the report obtained by Fox News Digital, the Restoration of America Foundation (ROAF) said Democrat-led states' shield laws — adopted to protect providers in blue states from being prosecuted by GOP state governments — allow providers to ship, or are being used by providers to ship, the abortion pill mifepristone into red states "with no in-person exam or verification of who takes them or whether they take them willingly." ROAF attributed the growth in mail-order abortions in part to FDA policy changes that suspended the in-person dispensing requirement during the COVID-19 pandemic before making the change permanent, allowing abortion drugs to be prescribed through telehealth and mailed to patients. BLUE STATE SHIELD LAWS ALLOWED 330K ABORTION PILLS TO BE SENT TO ABORTION BAN STATES, PRO-LIFE GROUP FINDS The report said nearly 15,000 medication abortions each month were provided under blue state shield laws by June 2025. It also said that by the end of 2024, about 15% of all U.S. abortions were through medication mailed to women in states with abortion restrictions. ROAF also cited an insurance claims analysis that the organization said found serious adverse health events following 10.9% of drug-induced abortions from 2017 through 2023, roughly 22 times the rate reported on the FDA-approved label for the abortion pill regimen. The group said the rate reached 11.2% in 2023 as the drugs were used more broadly. According to the report, ROAF estimated that mail-order drugs were "directly responsible" for more than 300,000 abortions in 2025 alone. This comes just ahead of the 110th anniversary of Planned Parenthood in the U.S., as the nation's largest abortion provider will be commemorating its Oct. 16, 1916, founding later this month. The ROAF report is urging Attorney General Todd Blanche to enforce the Comstock Act, an 1873 law criminalizing sending certain abortion-related materials that the pro-life group argues should be used by the Trump administration to stop shield laws from protecting mail-order medication abortions. "As we come up with this anniversary for Planned Parenthood, we think it's a good moment to release this paper. We really want to talk about the Comstock Act and the impact it could have on abortions going forward in this country," ROAF CEO Doug Truax told Fox News Digital. "The Comstock Act says it's illegal to put these drugs in the mail, so we're just asking them to enforce the law," he continued. After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, which returned the power to make abortion laws to the states, the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel under the Biden administration in December 2022 issued an opinion that concluded that the Comstock Act does not prohibit mailing mifepristone or misoprostol when the sender lacks intent that the recipient use the drugs unlawfully. The Biden administration's Office of Legal Counsel concluded in a December 2022 opinion that the Comstock Act does not prohibit mailing mifepristone or misoprostol when the sender lacks the intent that the drugs be used unlawfully. But Blanche said during his confirmation hearings over the summer that he would review how the DOJ interprets the Comstock Act. ROAF says the department should withdraw the Biden administration’s opinion, investigate providers and organizations involved in mailing the drugs and enforce the 150-year-old federal law, which the group argues would effectively ban the mailing of abortion drugs nationwide. PRO-LIFE GROUP FINDS BIDEN-ERA FDA POLICY IS DRIVING 500 ABORTIONS PER DAY, SAYS TRUMP HAS POWER TO END IT "We are asking the administration to take a step back and say, okay, when Roe was the law of the land, Comstock was unenforceable. But since Roe is out, Comstock is back on the table, and it is valid law, and it is illegal to put abortion drugs in the mail. You have thousands of people in basically blue states mailing a ton of pills around this country ... it's resulting in the amount of deaths that we're talking about here. So this is an illegal action that they're taking. We just want you to enforce Comstock, and it will save hundreds of thousands of lives going forward," Truax said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's a great way to get momentum back on our side in the pro-life community, which, frankly, I think the president and all conservatives around the country would appreciate now, as we head into November 3, and then, especially as we head into the next election cycle," he added.

articles.title: Kaliningrad is just Putin’s red herring
articles.summary: Moscow is hellbent on messaging to NATO that Kaliningrad — its exclave that is nestled between Poland and Lithuania on the Baltic Sea — is the new nuclear red line in Europe. In the wake of “The Wargame” — a British TV miniseries being aired by Sky News that explores the United Kingdom’s potential responses if…
articles.body:
Moscow is hellbent on messaging to NATO that Kaliningrad — its exclave that is nestled between Poland and Lithuania on the Baltic Sea — is the new nuclear red line in Europe.

In the wake of “ The Wargame ” — a British TV miniseries being aired by Sky News that explores the United Kingdom’s potential responses if attacked by Russia — the Kremlin sent a formal demarche to NATO, accusing the 32-member alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” by threatening Kaliningrad.

The Russian diplomatic note also declared that “Russia [is willing] to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory, should NATO countries undertake any attempt at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country.”

Brussels quickly brushed it off. NATO formally reminded Moscow that the organization is a defensive alliance and that “None of NATO’s exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation.”

NATO also called on Russia “to end its unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine” and “to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.”

It should have also called out Moscow’s misdirection and hypocrisy. The impetus for “The Wargame” series stems, in part, from repeated calls on Russian state-controlled media to nuke European capitals in retaliation for their support of Ukraine.

In September 2022, Olga Skabeyeva, known as “Putin’s Iron Doll,” agreed with her guest on Russia One’s “60 Minutes” that Russian President Vladimir Putin should have nuked Queen Elizabeth’s funeral and turned the United Kingdom into a “Martian wasteland.” Skabeyeva’s guest panelists lamented the missed opportunity, given that many world leaders, including then-President Joe Biden, were in attendance.

Four years later and Moscow is still at it. Margarita Simonyan, the head of the RT network and a Putin loyalist, accused the British media of playing “a little game of ‘Let’s pretend we’re going to war,’ terrifying their audience with fantasies of a clash with Russia.” Somewhat inconsistently, she then reiterated Moscow’s willingness to use nukes.

But it is Russia that is playing games here. Faced with ever-growing setbacks in Ukraine — Moscow is now not only suffering from strategic drone strikes but also losing captured territory due to Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi — Putin is desperately looking for new ways to end Europe’s support of Kyiv .

Russia’s kinetic hybrid war against Europe is one way. Nuclear bluffing — a card Moscow has played since the start of the war — is another. The only difference now is that Putin is attempting to make Kaliningrad the new flashpoint.

But in doing so, Putin is unwittingly showing vulnerability. Kaliningrad is a hollowed-out shell of what it was before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. As Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski pointed out earlier this month, “There are hardly any [Russian] troops [in the Kaliningrad exclave].”

Although Kaliningrad is still the headquarters of the Russian Baltic Fleet , the Baltic Sea itself has effectively become a NATO-controlled lake, after the accession of Sweden and Finland as the newest members of NATO.

Ostensibly, Kaliningrad’s primary defense is now its 100 or so nuclear-equipped Iskander-M missiles that are permanently based there. It has been denuded of most of its conventional military forces — including its once 12,000-strong 11th Army Corps — dispatched to Ukraine in 2022.

The 11th Army Corps still exists, but barely. It was mostly wrecked in Kharkiv during Ukraine’s successful 2022 counteroffensive.

Meanwhile, Kaliningrad — once rightly feared by Brussels as Russia’s unsinkable aircraft carrier strategically positioned in the middle of NATO territory — is highly vulnerable. Moscow’s nuclear Armageddon bluffing is simply the latest attempt by Putin and his Kremlin cronies to paper over this problem.

Nuclear bluffing aside, Russia is really just attempting to convince NATO it has military capabilities that now exist only in theory. In the past, Moscow has intentionally used Kaliningrad to threaten the Suwalki Gap — the 40-mile-wide land corridor connecting Poland and the other western NATO powers to their Baltic allies. Russia, every four years, conducts a joint military exercise with Belarus that often practices seizing this gap in order to cut Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia from the rest of NATO and its ground forces.

Notably, in 2025, this exercise included “a simulated use of [Russian] nuclear weapons.” Its strategic intent was clear enough: to bully Poland, the Baltic States, and the rest of Eastern Europe into submission.

Putin knows how the game is played. His armies ostentatiously practice attacking and defeating NATO, while Brussels conducts defensive exercises designed to simulate repelling Russian military forces from Europe. “The Wargame” — especially given that it was a harmless television show about a hypothetical — did not change the asymmetry of this situation.

Kaliningrad as the new red line is simply a Russian red herring. It is being used by Putin as domestic cover as his special military operation falters in Ukraine, and to deter NATO from responding to Russia’s growing kinetic hybrid war against the West.

Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: FAA breaks controller hiring record after chief warned system was ‘chronically understaffed’
articles.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration hired 2,235 air traffic controller trainees this fiscal year, smashing its all-time record amid staffing shortages.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The Federal Aviation Administration broke its all-time record for air traffic controller hiring this year, bringing on 2,235 trainees as the agency works to reverse years of staffing shortages across the nation. The FAA surpassed its fiscal year 2026 goal of hiring 2,200 air traffic controller trainees, marking the most hired in a single fiscal year in agency history, the Department of Transportation told Fox News Digital exclusively. The agency also reached its highest certified controller staffing level in a decade, with 11,027 certified professional controllers as of Sept. 30, up from 10,694 at the end of fiscal year 2025, according to the DOT. CBP TOUTS HISTORIC MILESTONE, PUSHES FOR EVEN LARGER WORKFORCE: 'WE AREN’T STOPPING HERE' "We’re recruiting, hiring, and training more air traffic controllers than ever before—and the numbers show it," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told Fox News Digital. "Thanks to President Trump, we've shaved months off the hiring pipeline, dramatically expanded our collegiate training programs, and inspired thousands of young gamers to pursue this exciting career," Duffy said. "This is an important milestone, but not the finish line as we work to reverse decades of staffing shortages." The record comes less than five months after the FAA unveiled an aggressive three-year workforce plan aimed at rebuilding a controller workforce strained by staffing shortages, mandatory overtime and lengthy training timelines. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had offered a stark assessment of the problem during congressional testimony last December, warning lawmakers that the agency would "never" reach adequate staffing under its previous structure. REAGAN NATIONAL AIRPORT MAKES DRASTIC CHANGE FOLLOWING DEADLY 2025 MIDAIR COLLISION "We’ll never catch up," Bedford said. "The system is designed to be chronically understaffed." The FAA's 2026-2028 Air Traffic Controller Workforce Plan, first reported by Fox News Digital in May, called for hiring 2,200 controller trainees in fiscal year 2026, 2,300 in fiscal year 2027 and 2,400 in fiscal year 2028. The agency finished the fiscal year 35 trainees above its first benchmark. The latest numbers also show growth among controllers who have completed training and become fully certified. The FAA entered fiscal year 2026 with 10,694 certified professional controllers and ended it with 11,027, a net increase of 333. The agency's workforce plan identifies 12,563 certified professional controllers as the staffing target needed to meet forecast demand. That leaves the FAA 1,536 certified controllers below its target as it enters fiscal year 2027. WHEN AIRLINE PILOTS SAY THERE ARE SAFETY ISSUES, WE NEED POLICYMAKERS TO LISTEN AND ACT The DOT told Fox News Digital it does not have an exact timeframe for reaching that benchmark, but said the administration is "supercharging" hiring and expanding its Enhanced Air Traffic Collegiate Training Initiative. The record follows another major hiring year in fiscal 2025, when the FAA brought on 2,028 controller trainees, its highest total since 2008. The administration has moved to accelerate the hiring and training pipeline as the FAA contends with retirements and other workforce losses. The FAA said in its May workforce plan that roughly 4,000 controllers were in the training pipeline at the time, including approximately 1,000 previously certified controllers training at new facilities. Becoming a fully certified controller can take more than two years for a new hire, depending on the complexity of the facility where they are assigned. The administration has also worked to retain experienced controllers while accelerating the pipeline for new ones. Nearly 400 retirement-eligible controllers were retained through a new bonus structure, while DOT says changes to the hiring process have shaved more than five months off the time it takes to bring on new recruits. The FAA has also expanded its Enhanced Air Traffic Collegiate Training Initiative, allowing qualified graduates of participating college programs to bypass the FAA Academy and report directly to facilities for on-the-job training. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The hiring surge comes as the Trump administration undertakes a broader overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system, backed by $12.5 billion for upgrades including telecommunications infrastructure, new radios and radars, and electronic flight strips. The FAA is also expanding simulator-based training and exploring artificial intelligence and machine learning tools to better manage air traffic demand. The record-setting year marks the first step in the FAA's three-year hiring push. The agency is targeting another 2,300 controller trainees in fiscal year 2027 and 2,400 in fiscal year 2028. articles.title: What to know about Trump’s deep red campaign blitz
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Trump kicks off trip in Texas ▪ Senate leaves town ahead of midterms ▪ Fed’s internal review clears Powell ▪ U.S. withdraws fully from Iraq President Trump is set to embark on a five-state swing through traditionally friendly Republican territory starting today, kicking off a midterm campaign push with Election Day…
articles.body:
President Trump is set to embark on a five-state swing through traditionally friendly Republican territory starting today, kicking off a midterm campaign push with Election Day just a little more than a month away.

Some of the states where the president is heading are home to among the most hotly contested races this year. But as The Hill’s Julia Manchester reports , he’s also raising some eyebrows with trips to deep-red states, including Alabama and Nebraska.

Republicans say there are benefits to be reaped from Trump’s visits to energize the base broadly, even if some of the visits are to states that are friendly to him.

Here’s a rundown on Trump’s upcoming stops:

The president’s tour will get started Thursday afternoon when he visits a manufacturing facility in the city of Denton, located in the northern part of the state.

Trump will visit Peterbilt Motors Company’s factory and tout his economic record, including what he describes as the resurgence of American manufacturing.

While Texas is a red state, it’s also the site of an extremely competitive Senate race between Democratic state Rep. James Talarico and Texas state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R). Polls have shown Talarico ahead; if he wins, it would be a huge victory for his party, which has not held a Senate seat in Texas since former Sen. Lloyd Bentsen served.

Talarico needs to overcome a Republican onslaught that’s been focused on helping to boost Paxton, with Trump’s super PAC spending millions to support the Republican nominee in recent weeks.

Democrats are also hopeful they can make gains in the House in Texas. A GOP redistricting effort was supposed to make that difficult, but with Hispanic voters moving away from the GOP, Democrats think they have some opportunities.

Trump’s visit to Oklahoma is unique in that — with less than five weeks to go before Election Day — the president is going to a state not seen as a battleground, even if a massive blue wave were to come.

The trip taking place later in the day Thursday will be Trump’s first to the Sooner State since 2020. He sent a welcome message to the state in a video posted to the social platform X ahead of the stop.

Oklahoma does have a pair of major statewide races this year with an open gubernatorial race and a Senate race following Markwayne Mullin ’s resignation to lead the Department of Homeland Security. The state has five House races, but none of them are expected to be competitive.

All five are rated as “solid Republican” by the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report.

Trump is following up the Oklahoma visit with another visit to a bright red state on Friday, going to Mobile for a rally at the University of South Alabama.

The state also has Senate and gubernatorial races that aren’t expected to be competitive. A Republican source told Manchester previously that Trump’s visits to the red states aren’t indicative that the races are competitive, noting Oklahoma and Alabama are close to the Texas and Florida media markets, respectively.

But at least one House race could potentially come into play in November.

Rep. Shomari Figures (D) is attempting to overcome long odds after state Republicans redrew Alabama’s congressional lines to help the party pick up a seat. Figures’s current district includes Mobile, though the district will be based in the state’s southeastern quadrant starting with this year’s elections.

While that race isn’t likely to determine which party wins the House majority, if a major Democratic wave emerges, Figures may have a slim chance of overcoming the gerrymander and winning a House seat.

Democrats are hoping to win back the governor’s mansion and a Senate seat in Ohio.

Trump will travel to Vandalia, which is just north of Dayton, to stump for Sen. Jon Husted (R), who is trying to fend off a comeback attempt from former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D).

The former senator narrowly lost his reelection bid two years ago despite Trump’s comfortable victory in the state, and Democrats are hopeful that Brown is exactly the right candidate to win a seat back.

Meanwhile, Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy are locked in a close race for the governor’s mansion. Ramaswamy had been one of Trump’s rivals in the 2024 Republican primaries but became one of his close allies, giving Trump a personal connection to the state.

Nebraska comes off as a state in line with Oklahoma and Alabama given its solid red history, but this year it seems like it could be in play.

Democrats are once again throwing their support behind Independent Dan Osborn , who unsuccessfully challenged Sen. Deb Fischer (R) in 2024. Now, he’s trying again against Sen. Pete Ricketts (R).

Osborn has said he wouldn’t caucus with either party, but Democrats want to take Ricketts out. Trump is expected to tie the independent candidate to the left during his remarks.

Senate Democrats on Thursday blocked legislation sponsored by Ricketts to restrict members of Congress from buying new stocks of publicly traded companies. The Senate GOP scheduled the vote on the Stop Insider Trading Act, which failed to meet the 60-vote threshold in a 53-47 vote, to help Ricketts.

Osborn has accused Ricketts of profiting from his stock portfolio, and the bill is an effort by Ricketts to play defense but also go on offense against Democrats for blocking the measure.

Nebraska is also home to a key House race. Democrats are counting on flipping Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District on their road to winning back the House majority.

Former Nebraska Rep. Hal Daub (R) , who used to represent the district, said Trump’s visit is about making sure Republicans aren’t sleeping on the midterms.

“The president’s trip is designed, I think, to energize that particular set of voters to be sure they cast their absentee ballot or turn out in the polls here in about 30 days, and I think that’s going to be positive,” he said. “I think on balance, that’s going to be positive.”

There are more opportunities on the board for Democrats to flip GOP-held seats than those for Republicans to flip Democratic-held seats in this cycle. But there are chances for the GOP. For a deep-dive look at where Republicans might win back some seats, subscribe to The Hill Insider and read Julia Mueller’s story on the 10 Democratic-held House seats most likely to flip.

▪ The Hill : The Republicans backing Democratic candidates in the midterms.

For a one-stop shop for all polling and forecast data ahead of the midterms: The Hill now has a new webpage tracking the numbers from our partner, Decision Desk HQ. The page shows which party is favored in the House and Senate, governor’s races, the president’s approval rating and more.

Click the link here to explore everything from The Hill’s Election Center.

Trump heads to Oklahoma today to kick off a travel sprint to the midterms. Oklahoma is a handful of politically red states the president will be visiting in the coming days, which also includes Florida. I asked Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) if he has any concerns about the president visiting Republican strongholds down the stretch.

“No, I mean, he’s going to go out and he’s got a lot to brag about. He can talk about how much he’s cut taxes, how we’re adding jobs, how the economy is growing,” Scott told me. “I think it’s great that he’s going to go out there and campaign and help our candidates,” he added.

Republicans had been planning at this point to sell their tax bill heading into November, but what’s currently rising to the top for voters are things they didn’t anticipate when the bill passed last year: war, high gas prices, and inflation that just won’t go away.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) ordered the scheduled execution of Christa Pike to be halted for at least the rest of the year after two attempts to execute her by lethal injection failed Wednesday night. Lee ordered an investigation into what occurred as Pike was still recorded to be breathing after receiving two doses of pentobarbital. The botched execution followed a legal fight that saw the Supreme Court on Wednesday night allow Pike’s execution over the objections of the three liberal justices.

Pennsylvania recorded its fifth measles-associated death on Wednesday, amid an ongoing outbreak that has become the worst Pennsylvania has seen in more than 35 years. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has refused to accept the state’s death count, instead counting only its second measles-related death this week.

The Senate voted to confirm Keith Sonderling to be permanent Labor secretary in a 47-41 party-line vote, filling a vacancy in Trump’s Cabinet. Sonderling, who is generally seen as employer-friendly, has been serving in the acting role since his predecessor, Lori Chavez-DeRemer, resigned earlier this year amid investigations into her and members of her family. The Senate adjourned for the midterm elections not long after the vote. We’ll get into that below.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) walks with reporters as he heads to a closed-door GOP lunch, at the Capitol in Washington, Sept. 30, 2026. (J. Scott Applewhite, Associated Press)

GOING HOME : The Senate adjourned Wednesday after holding its final votes before the midterms in November, leaving a laundry list of unfinished legislative items that Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has decided to punt until after Election Day.

The day was marked by a couple of high-profile legislative blocks by Democrats, who argued the GOP-backed bills did not go far enough. But in blocking the legislation, Democrats were also depriving GOP candidates of legislative victories.

The first example was the Ricketts legislation on stock trades, while the second bill, the Ratepayer Protection Act, was backed by Husted.

Husted has come under attacks from Brown, his Democratic opponent, over the building of data centers in Ohio. That bill also failed to meet the 60-vote threshold in a 57-43 vote after four Democrats joined Republicans to back the legislation seeking to address voter concerns about data centers and energy costs.

The data center bill requires utility regulators to consider adopting a federal standard that would hold large companies responsible for the costs of new energy infrastructure used for data centers, rather than passing those costs onto consumers.

Democrats argued in both cases that the bills didn’t go far enough.

“Only Senate Republicans would dare call a bill that permits members of Congress to continue to own, sell and, in some instances, buy stocks a stock-trading ban. They can’t be serious. The Republican bill is a permission slip for corruption, not a stock-trading ban,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said on the Senate floor.

But make no mistake, election-year politics were also in play in both cases.

There were some examples of bipartisanship on Wednesday.

The Hill’s Rachel Frazin has a look at senators’ long-awaited permitting reform deal, which Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) announced yesterday after months of negotiations. They say the agreement will speed up the construction of the nation’s energy and infrastructure projects while reining in costs from data centers. Subscribe to The Hill Insider for Frazin’s reporting on the negotiation process, what the White House is saying and where senators go from here.

Thune has left several must-pass pieces of legislation to the lame-duck, The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports , noting senators will only have four full weeks when they return in November to pass the farm bill, FISA reauthorization, the annual defense authorization bill, 12 regular appropriations bills, a permitting reform bill, and an emergency supplemental defense spending package for the Pentagon, whse stockpile of weapons and munitions has been depleted after months of war with Iran.

STATE OF THE FORCE : Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth invited governors to bid for their states to host the “next great American” base built in the U.S., during his “State of the Force” speech at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia.

“We’re calling on every governor in the country and adjutant general, every tag across this great republic, to step up to the plate and bring us their best sales pitch,” Hegseth told junior officers and enlisted leaders gathered to hear his address, the second year he’s given such a speech.

“If your state wants the honor of hosting 15,000 to 25,000 of America’s great troops, show us why and how you’re going to do it, cutting through the red tape, offering up the land, and rolling out the red carpet for our military families,” the Defense secretary continued.

Hegseth also announced the 20 percent reduction in its generals and admirals, which the Pentagon had previewed the day before, and touted his efforts to rid the military of “woke” culture.

Hegseth said he is creating a four-star combatant command for autonomous warfare, which will overhaul the way the Pentagon buys and deploys drones and robotics. He also announced efforts to study the future of warfare, a task that would be helmed by SpaceX and xAI CEO Elon Musk , Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.).

‘STRONG INDICATIONS’: United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are “strong indications” Iran was involved in the security incident Sunday near the U.S.-run military air base in England.

“There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation,” Burnham told the BBC in an interview yesterday.

Burnham said U.K. and U.S. forces are working closely together on the investigation into the incident, which saw five men arrested on suspicion of explosives offenses and planning an act of terror, before they were released on bail the next day. Police said they found some accelerate, gasoline, in the vans but no explosives.

Burnham said he would update the public “in due course.” Iran has denied involvement in the incident.

NO REASONABLE GROUNDS : The Federal Reserve’s internal watchdog found no evidence of criminality in its probe into the institution’s handling of its multimillion-dollar renovation project, breaking with the Department of Justice (DOJ), which had launched an investigation into the Fed’s former chair, Jerome Powell .

The report released Wednesday from the office of Inspector General Michael Horowitz acknowledged that the Fed hasn’t “effectively executed” the construction management risk contract for two of its buildings in the nation’s capital. But the report said no reasonable grounds were found to suggest any federal law had been violated.

Horowitz opened the investigation in April at the recommendation of Jeanine Pirro , the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia. Pirro had led an investigation into Powell for months before she handed it off to Horowitz in the face of bipartisan pressure.

Powell had hit back against the DOJ and the president, accusing Trump of using the investigation as a prelude to get him to be more aggressive in lowering interest rates.

Trump slammed Powell after the report came out, calling on him to resign from his post as Fed governor. Powell’s term as chair has since come to an end.

The president said he’s instructing Attorney General Todd Blanche to “study” the report and “make a determination as what to do” concerning the cost overruns.

CHECKS IN THE MAIL : The White House has begun mailing out $500 refund checks to about 1 million Americans who the Trump administration says were overcharged for their insurance through ObamaCare.

An administration official said Treasury Department checks will start going out to Americans across 30 states that use healthcare.gov, the federal marketplace where users can sign up for ObamaCare health insurance.

The move comes as the administration is looking for wins on healthcare and affordability with Election Day fast approaching.

“For years, the Biden administration overcharged you to fund the operation of HealthCare.gov,” Trump wrote in a letter accompanying the checks that was shared with The Hill. “That money belongs to hard-working Americans, not the Government, and now I’m returning it to you!”

Direct payments to consumers are a key part of Trump’s healthcare plan. He’s promoted taking money away from ObamaCare subsidies and providing it back to Americans to let them pay directly for insurance.

The announcement came weeks after a task force led by Vice President Vance revealed it plans to remove close to 760,000 people from Affordable Care Act (ACA) coverage because of allegedly fraudulent enrollment.

The president also unveiled a platform called TrumpRx in February as a resource for consumers to download coupons for certain drugs to take to pharmacies and receive discounts.

But the refund checks will only help a small subset of people. There are 19.2 million people enrolled in ACA coverage, and people who still get premium subsidies aren’t eligible. People who live in the mostly blue-leaning states that operate their own exchanges also aren’t eligible.

Most of the recipients of the checks will be for people who earn 400 percent of the federal poverty level, meaning $64,000 for a single person or $132,000 for a family of four.

These individuals no longer receive financial assistance to help them afford premiums as the enhanced ACA subsidies expired at the end of last year.

MIDFLIGHT DIVERSION :Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said a pilot aboard a diverted Flydubai flight was arrested after allegedly stabbing his co-pilot, forcing others on board to interfere to prevent the plane from crashing.

The flight was headed to Tel Aviv but was diverted to Saudi Arabia, where officials are interrogating the suspect, Netanyahu said yesterday. All passengers landed safely.

“During the flight, as they were approaching Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently attempted to crash the plane with everyone on board,” Netanyahu said, according to an unofficial translation of his remarks. “Additional flight crew on board entered the cockpit and managed to stabilize the aircraft.”

The flight dropped 14,000 feet in less than a minute, according to an altitude path by Flight Radar, before a passenger “managed to break into the cockpit together with one of the crew members, and … together they neutralized the pilot who carried out the stabbing while he was attempting to sabotage the aircraft’s systems,” Netanyahu said, recounting a conversation he had with the Israeli passenger.

Netanyahu said he has “instructed the security establishment to prepare for additional potential threats” in Israel and Saudi Arabia.

While Netanyahu characterized the incident as a highly severe security incident, some Israeli officials took a step further, including Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who called the incident an alleged attempted hijacking by a “terrorist.”

articles.title: Revenge of the citizens: Let’s text the candidates back, asking them for money
articles.summary: Every time you get a text or email from a politician or political group asking for money, write them back, asking for money.
articles.body:
I have been scolded by Hakeem Jeffries, with him saying, “I asked once. I asked twice. I asked a third time. I’m asking again today.”

And from the man who has access to the nuclear codes, I got a message, “My phone’s battery is on 5 percent, so this has to be quick. I sent you an invitation to my Inner Circle, but I haven’t heard back. I want you to advise me! Your final deadline to accept is in 15 minutes.”

And another one from Trump: “Wake up… ALL HELL IS ABOUT TO BREAK LOOSE! Will you do one final favor for me before it’s too late? If you help me out RIGHT HERE RIGHT NOW, I’ll have my team add your name to my Inner Circle Roster, where you can begin advising me on what my top priorities should be.”

J.D. Vance, Ted Cruz, Chuck Schumer, Bernie Sanders, Jim Jordan, Kamala Harris and dozens of others respect me, want my opinion, are making sure I’m the first to know, think I’m essential and — oh, yeah, by the way — want money. The Vaccine Advisory Board chastised me with “Are you getting my texts? You still haven’t responded. I’m reaching out … one last time.” Even the mayor of Chicago thinks I want to support him.

Pols, PACs and special interest groups on both sides clog my email accounts and blow up my phone with pleas and dire threats. The threat is that the country will be ruined unless I immediately send them money. And more money. And more money.

I hit Stop and Block Spam, to no avail. Jeffries, for example, has sent me pleas from six different phone numbers. I have gotten as many as 10 texts and eight emails in one day.

After giving to one politician and then seeing an upsurge, I wrote to her saying I would give again only if I was guaranteed my name would not be shared. She did not respond.

I must question whether this is truly an effective way to raise money, at the cost of alienating voters who might have otherwise been supportive. As opposed to the shrill, flattering ones like this from Michael Whatley: “Who are the battle-tested patriots in our corner who will give me the unvarnished truth about what they are seeing on the ground? Your name was at the very top of the ledger.”

Well, I had no idea! But then there are the flagrantly manipulative ones like, “Do you want Donald Trump’s face on your money? Please complete the poll or be marked yes.”

I know I am not the only one and propose a major pushback: Every time you get a text or email from a politician or political group asking for money, write them back, asking for money.

“Hello Fellow Patriot,” I might write. “I am several thousand dollars short of my first of the month funding deadline. I know you care about me since you have written to me so many times. Would you be willing to send me a few hundred dollars to push me on to victory over debt?

Or, “Dear Concerned Citizen: My landlord has raised my rent, the cost of fuel is soaring, and a trip to the grocery store tests my credit card balance. Can you help me with this dire financial crisis? As an elected official, I know you have access to more funding than I do. Send as much as you can, but any amount is appreciated.”

Or how about: “Greetings Respected American. This is not a request for money, as I am sure you get too many of those. I’m just looking for your opinion on issues impacting our country today. Do you feel our country is headed in the right direction? I didn’t think so. Are you willing to contribute as little as $100 to help get us back on track?”:

For all of these messages, or whatever ones you come up with, be sure to include your Zelle, Venmo or Paypal information. I suspect you won’t get a cent back, but maybe we can be as annoying to them as they are to us.

And we might even turn it into a group effort. Alas, I know the name “Citizens United” has already been taken.

Mark Schorr is the author of a dozen novels. Many decades ago, he served as the press spokesperson for a New York State assemblyman who was subsequently convicted of fraud and sent to prison.
